entries.q: Can cats get rabies too, or only dogs?
entries.a:
Cats can get rabies and pass it to people through bites and scratches. Rabies can infect all mammals.

The Anti-Rabies Act (RA 9482) mainly talks about dogs, but DOH offices urge owners to vaccinate both dogs and cats against rabies regularly and not let them roam freely. The national campaign theme is "Rabies-free na pusa't aso, kaligtasan ng pamilyang Pilipino."

Ask your vet about your cat's yearly anti-rabies shot, and treat any cat bite or scratch seriously.

entries.q: Is anti-rabies treatment for people free?
entries.a:
Under Section 6 of RA 9482, the DOH must provide post-exposure treatment for bite victims at minimum cost, and free pre-exposure shots for high-risk workers. Free routine shots are also given to schoolchildren aged 5 to 14 in high-risk areas (Section 4).

Costs can still differ between government and private Animal Bite Treatment Centers, so ask your local health center or ABTC. Never skip treatment because of cost. And if a dog bit you, its owner is required by law to pay your medical expenses (Section 5).

entries.q: Is it illegal to abandon my pet?
entries.a:
Yes. RA 10631, which amended the Animal Welfare Act, added a rule against abandoning animals.

- Leaving your pet, for good or even for a while, without a good reason and without arranging for its care counts as maltreatment
- If abandonment leads to the animal suffering or dying, the owner faces the maximum penalty

If you can no longer care for your pet, look for a new home or ask a rescue group or shelter for help instead of leaving it on the street.

entries.q: What's the penalty for animal cruelty in the Philippines?
entries.a:
Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

entries.q: Where can I report animal abuse or neglect?
entries.a:
Under the Animal Welfare Act as amended by RA 10631 (Section 10):

- The Philippine National Police (PNP), the NBI and other law enforcement agencies have animal welfare enforcement officers
- The Secretary of Agriculture can deputize trained volunteers and members of NGOs and community groups as enforcement officers
- These officers can rescue maltreated animals and arrest violators

LGUs are also required to enforce the anti-cruelty rules of RA 8485 (RA 9482, Section 7). You can report to the police, your LGU, or an animal welfare group. Take photos or videos and note the date and place to help your report.

entries.q: Can a pet legally be put to sleep in the Philippines?
entries.a:
Only for reasons the Animal Welfare Act allows. Section 6 of RA 8485 permits killing a pet when, for example:

- A licensed vet certifies it has an incurable communicable disease
- A licensed vet certifies it is needed to end the animal's suffering
- It is needed to prevent immediate danger to human life or limb

It must be done humanely, using methods approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare. Electrocution of dogs is banned under RA 9482. Talk to your vet if you're facing this decision.

entries.q: What papers do I need to bring my dog or cat to another island or province?
entries.a:
You need a local shipping permit from the Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), applied for online at nvqsd.bai.gov.ph. Under the BAI Citizen's Charter, dogs and cats need:

- A veterinary health certificate from a licensed vet, showing rabies vaccine details (brand, batch/lot number, date given, next due date)
- A rabies vaccination certificate signed by the vet with their PRC number
- The pet should be about 3 to 4 months old or older
- The rabies shot should be at least 14 days and not more than 1 year old (annual boosters can ship right away)

The permit is free; processing takes up to 3 working days. Rules may change, so confirm with BAI before your trip.

entries.q: Are there rules on how my pet should be transported, like by van or boat?
entries.a:
Yes. Section 4 of the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485) sets rules for transporting animals:

- Carriers must provide clean, sanitary facilities for animals
- Animals must get food and water on trips longer than 12 hours, or when needed
- Overcrowding, cruel confinement and putting animals in vehicle trunks count as cruelty

A BAI permit is required to transport animals. For pets, apply for a BAI local shipping permit before your trip, and prepare a vet health certificate and rabies vaccination certificate.

entries.q: My dog is breathing very fast and his gums look pale. What should I do?
entries.a:
Fast breathing with pale gums can mean shock, blood loss or a heart or lung problem. Go to a vet now.

While you get there:
- Keep him calm and still, and carry him if you can
- Keep him at a comfortable temperature, not too hot
- Don't give food, water or any medicine

Call the clinic on the way so they're ready for you.

entries.q: My cat had a seizure that lasted about 2 minutes. She seems okay now.
entries.a:
A seizure always needs a vet check, even if she seems fine now. Call your vet today, and go straight away if she has another one, or if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes.

Until then:
- Keep her somewhere quiet and dim, away from stairs
- If it happens again, don't hold her or put anything in her mouth
- Time it and, if you can, take a video for the vet

Tell the vet about anything she could have eaten, such as medicines, insecticides or plants.

entries.q: My dog's belly is swollen and he keeps trying to vomit but nothing comes out.
entries.a:
A swollen belly with retching that brings nothing up can be bloat (stomach twisting). It can kill within hours. Go to a vet now.

- Don't wait to see if it passes
- Don't give food, water or medicine
- Call the clinic on the way so they can prepare

Bloat is more common in large, deep-chested dogs, and after a big meal or exercise.

entries.q: My cat licked a lily flower. Is that dangerous?
entries.a:
Yes. Lilies are very poisonous to cats. Even licking the pollen or drinking the vase water can cause kidney failure. Go to a vet now, even if she seems fine, because treatment works best in the first hours.

- Bring the plant or a photo of it
- Wipe pollen off her fur and face with a damp cloth so she doesn't lick more
- Don't make her vomit unless the vet tells you to

Keep lilies out of any home with cats.

entries.q: Can dogs eat grapes?
entries.a:
No. Grapes and raisins can cause sudden kidney failure in dogs, and even a few can be dangerous for some dogs. There's no safe amount.

If your dog ate grapes or raisins:
- Go to a vet now, even if they seem fine
- Tell the vet how many and when

Safer treats include small pieces of plain cooked chicken, carrot or apple without the seeds.

entries.q: When should my puppy get the anti-rabies vaccine?
entries.a:
Puppies usually get their first anti-rabies shot at about 3 months old, then boosters as your vet advises, usually every year. In the Philippines, the Anti-Rabies Act requires dogs to be vaccinated against rabies.

- Many LGUs hold free anti-rabies vaccination drives, so ask your barangay or city vet
- Keep the vaccination card, because you may need it for travel or boarding
- Your puppy also needs the core puppy shots (such as 5-in-1), which your vet will schedule

entries.q: How do I know if my dog has ticks?
entries.a:
Check your dog by running your hands slowly over the whole body. Ticks feel like small bumps and like to hide:
- In and around the ears
- Between the toes
- Around the neck, armpits and groin

Other signs are scratching, small scabs, or ticks in your dog's bed. Ticks can spread serious blood diseases such as ehrlichiosis, which is common in the Philippines. See a vet if your dog is weak, has pale gums, a fever or nosebleeds.

Ask your vet for a tick prevention product that suits your dog's weight, and treat the yard and bedding too.

entries.q: How many times a day should I feed my kitten?
entries.a:
Kittens have small stomachs and grow fast, so feed small meals often:
- Up to about 6 months: 3-4 meals a day
- After 6 months: 2 meals a day

Use food made for kittens, and follow the amount on the pack for their weight. Always leave fresh water. Don't give cow's milk, because many cats can't digest it and get diarrhea.

Ask your vet to check their weight at each vaccination visit.

entries.q: Is it okay to give my dog leftover rice and fish bones?
entries.a:
Plain rice is fine now and then, but fish bones are not. Cooked bones can splinter and get stuck in the mouth, throat or gut.

- Remove all bones before sharing fish
- Avoid salty, oily or spicy leftovers, and anything with onion or garlic
- Leftovers alone aren't a complete diet, so base meals on a balanced dog food

If your dog swallowed a bone and is gagging, drooling, vomiting or seems in pain, see a vet.

entries.q: How do I clean my dog's ears?
entries.a:
Clean only when the ears look dirty, often about once every 1-2 weeks.
- Use an ear cleaner for dogs, not alcohol or hydrogen peroxide
- Fill the ear canal as the label says, massage the base of the ear, and let your dog shake
- Wipe the outer part with cotton or gauze
- Don't push cotton buds into the canal

See a vet if you notice a bad smell, redness, swelling, dark discharge, head shaking or pain, which can mean an infection.

entries.q: My cat scratches the sofa. How can I stop it?
entries.a:
Scratching is normal for cats. It keeps their claws healthy and marks their space, so give them a better place to do it.
- Put a sturdy scratching post next to the sofa, tall enough for a full stretch
- Try both upright posts and flat cardboard scratchers
- Reward your cat with treats or play when they use it
- Cover the sofa spots with a throw or double-sided tape for a while
- Trim the claws regularly

Don't punish or declaw your cat.

entries.q: My dog barks a lot when I leave the house.
entries.a:
This is often separation anxiety: your dog is stressed being alone.
- Give a good walk and play before you leave
- Practise short absences, then make them slowly longer
- Leave a safe chew toy or a food puzzle
- Keep leaving and coming home calm and low-key
- Don't punish the barking, because it adds to the stress

If your dog also destroys things, soils the house or hurts themselves, talk to your vet or a trainer. Some dogs need a behavior plan.

entries.q: How many mg of amoxicillin can I give my 10 kg dog?
entries.a:
I can't give medicine doses. Antibiotics need a vet's exam and prescription, because the right medicine and dose depend on what the infection is and on your dog's health.

- Don't use leftover or human antibiotics, as the wrong one or the wrong dose can make things worse
- See your vet, who can examine your dog and prescribe the right treatment

If your dog is very weak, not eating, or has trouble breathing, go to a vet now.

entries.q: Can I give my cat ibuprofen?
entries.a:
No. Ibuprofen and other human pain medicines, such as paracetamol and aspirin, are poisonous to cats. Even one tablet can cause stomach bleeding and kidney failure.

If your cat already took some, go to a vet now. If your cat seems to be in pain, see your vet, who can give a medicine that is safe for cats.

entries.q: My cat hasn't eaten for 2 days.
entries.a:
Two days without food is serious for a cat. Cats can quickly develop a liver problem (hepatic lipidosis) when they stop eating. Take her to a vet today.

- Note anything else you've seen, such as vomiting, hiding, drooling or litter box changes
- Don't force-feed her

Go now if she is also vomiting, very weak, breathing hard, or is a male cat straining to pee.

entries.q: My dog has a deep cut on his leg and it won't stop bleeding.
entries.a:
Heavy bleeding is an emergency. Head to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, and control the bleeding on the way.

- Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze, using your palm or fingers.
- Wrap a bandage over it snugly, but not so tight that it cuts off circulation.
- If blood soaks through, don't pull the cloth off. Add more layers on top and keep pressing.
- Tape the outer layer so it stays in place while you travel.

Pain can make even a gentle dog bite. A soft cloth muzzle can protect you, but only if he is breathing normally. Have someone else drive so you can keep pressure on the wound. Pale gums, weakness or fast breathing can mean shock, so tell the clinic when you call.

entries.q: My dog threw up and there was blood in it. Is that an emergency?
entries.a:
Treat it as one. Blood in vomit can come from bleeding in the stomach or gut, ulcers caused by human pain relievers, rat poison, or swallowed chemicals. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now and go in, especially if your dog keeps vomiting, is weak, has pale gums or a painful belly.

What to do:
- Don't give any human medicine.
- Don't try to make him vomit.
- Bring any packaging of medicine, poison or chemical he might have gotten into.
- Take a photo of the vomit to show the vet.

On the way, keep him calm and watch his gums and breathing.

entries.q: My dog chewed open a bottle of ibuprofen and swallowed some tablets.
entries.a:
Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now. Human pain relievers like ibuprofen, naproxen and aspirin (NSAIDs) are dangerous for dogs. They can cause stomach ulcers, bleeding and kidney damage, and large amounts can cause seizures or coma.

Signs may include vomiting, diarrhea, black stools, belly pain, not eating, weakness and pale gums.

Before you go:
- Bring the bottle and count how many tablets are missing, so the vet can judge the risk.
- Only make your dog vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Don't give any other medicine.

On the way, keep him calm and watch for vomiting or weakness. Never give human pain medicine to a pet without your vet's advice.

entries.q: My dog licked some liquid that leaked from the car radiator. Is coolant dangerous?
entries.a:
Yes, very. Most antifreeze or coolant contains ethylene glycol, which tastes sweet and can kill pets even in small amounts. Cats are affected by even less than dogs. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic immediately. Treatment works best in the first few hours, before the kidneys are damaged.

Early signs look like drunkenness: wobbling, vomiting, and drinking and peeing a lot. Dogs may seem better after about 12 hours, but the poison is still working. Kidney failure can follow within about 1.5 to 3 days in dogs and 12 to 24 hours in cats.

Before you go:
- Bring the coolant bottle if you have it.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm. Later, clean up the spill and cover it with cat litter or sand.

entries.q: Is it safe to use an essential oil diffuser if I have a cat?
entries.a:
Be careful. Concentrated essential oils can poison pets if they lick them, step in them, or get them on their fur. Never put essential oils directly on your cat or dog, and keep bottles and diffusers where pets can't knock them over. Concentrated tea tree oil can cause problems with just a few drops. Liquid potpourri is also risky, especially for cats, who lick it off their fur.

A diffuser used briefly in a room your pet can't enter is less likely to cause trouble. Skip it if your pet has breathing problems.

If your pet gets oil on the skin or fur, or seems wobbly, dull, weak or vomits, call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and go in. Move your pet to fresh air, bring the bottle, and only make your pet vomit if a vet tells you to.

entries.q: Can I walk my puppy outside before his vaccines are finished?
entries.a:
Early socializing is very important for your puppy's behavior, and experts say it can start before the vaccine series is done, as long as you do it carefully.

Until your vet says your puppy is fully protected:
- Avoid places where unknown dogs pee and poop, like parks, sidewalks and pet store floors
- Let him meet only healthy puppies and fully vaccinated adult dogs
- Carry him if you want him to see new sights, sounds and people
- Use a clean, safe place for supervised puppy play

Parvovirus can survive for a long time in places where infected dogs have been, so stay away from those spots. Ask your vet when it is safe to walk your puppy normally.
entries.src: WSAVA 2024 Guidelines for the Vaccination of Dogs and Cats

entries.q: Can I catch worms from my dog or cat?
entries.a:
Yes, some can spread to people:
- Roundworm eggs in soil or poop can be swallowed, mostly by children, and the larvae can harm the eyes or organs
- Hookworm larvae in soil can go into bare skin and cause an itchy, winding rash
- Some tapeworms can infect people too

To protect your family:
- Pick up dog poop right away, including in your yard
- Scoop the litter box every day
- Wash hands with soap and water after handling pets, poop or soil
- Cover sandboxes and wear gloves when gardening
- Keep your pets on the deworming plan your vet recommends

If a family member is unwell, talk to a doctor.

entries.q: My dog keeps scratching. Could it be fleas?
entries.a:
It could be. Common flea signs include:
- Scratching, biting or licking the skin a lot
- Hair loss or red skin near the tail and between or behind the legs
- Small red bumps or flaky skin
- Seeing adult fleas or "flea dirt" (tiny black specks of flea poop) in the fur

Some pets are allergic to flea bites, which makes the itching worse. A heavy flea load can cause blood loss (anemia). Fleas also spread tapeworms.

Itching can have other causes too, like mites or allergies, so have your vet check your dog. Ask your vet for a flea product that suits your dog's weight and age.

entries.q: How do I safely remove a tick from my dog?
entries.a:
Remove ticks as soon as you find them:
- Use fine-tipped tweezers and grip the tick as close to the skin as you can
- Pull straight out with slow, steady pressure. Don't twist or jerk
- Don't use bare hands, matches, heat, nail polish or petroleum jelly
- Don't crush the tick. Drop it in rubbing alcohol, seal it in a bag or wrap it in tape
- Wash the bite area and your hands with soap and water

If small mouthparts stay in the skin, it usually heals on its own.

Watch the spot for a few days. See your vet if it gets red or swollen, if your dog has many ticks, or if he seems unwell in the weeks after.

entries.q: I found a lump on my senior dog. Should I just watch it?
entries.a:
Lumps are more common as pets age. Many are harmless fatty lumps, but some are cancers that look and feel exactly the same. Senior care guidelines warn that simply waiting and watching can be risky.

What to do:
- Book a vet visit soon
- Your vet may take a small needle sample to see what the lump is made of
- Note its size and take a photo so changes can be tracked

See a vet sooner if the lump grows quickly, bleeds or bothers your dog. Also check the mouth, eyes and toes, since growths there can be missed.

Finding a problem early usually means more treatment options.

entries.q: My dog got caught by the dog pound. How do I get him back?
entries.a:
Under Section 9 of RA 9482, unregistered, stray or unvaccinated dogs can be impounded by the LGU. Go to your city or municipal pound or veterinary office as soon as possible.

- Dogs not claimed within 3 days (72 hours) may be put up for adoption or otherwise disposed of
- To claim your dog, you pay a fee to the LGU; the law sets the release fine at P500 to P1,000 (Section 11)
- A dog impounded 3 times is released only after being spayed or neutered, at the owner's cost (Section 10)

Bring proof of ownership and vaccination if you have it. These amounts are as written in the 2007 law. Your city or municipality may have its own ordinance, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

entries.q: My dog bit someone. What does the law say I need to do?
entries.a:
Under Section 5 of RA 9482, the owner must:

- Report the bite to the concerned officials (for example your barangay or city/municipal veterinary or health office) within 24 hours
- Place the dog under observation by a government or private veterinarian
- Help the person who was bitten right away, and pay for their medical and related expenses

Tell the person to wash the wound and go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center promptly.

Refusing to have the dog observed carries a fine of P10,000, or P25,000 if you also refuse to pay the victim's medical costs (Section 11). Local amounts may differ, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

entries.q: how many days do i need to observe my dog after it bit someone?
entries.a:
The implementing rules of RA 9482 set a 14-day observation period. During those 14 days the dog must not be killed or put to sleep.

- Keep the dog confined and have it checked by a government or private vet (Section 5 of RA 9482)
- If the dog dies during observation, the owner must bring it in right away for a rabies laboratory test

The person who was bitten should not wait for the observation to finish before getting care. They should go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center promptly.

entries.q: When is Rabies Awareness Month in the Philippines?
entries.a:
March. Executive Order No. 84, signed in 1999, declared March of every year as Rabies Awareness Month. It calls for a nationwide rabies information drive and mass dog vaccination with free vaccines.

The implementing rules of RA 9482 also mark March as Rabies Awareness Month, and September 28 as World Rabies Day.

Many LGUs hold free vaccination and pet registration activities in March, so it's a good time to update your pet's shots.

entries.q: What counts as animal cruelty under Philippine law?
entries.a:
Under Section 6 of the Animal Welfare Act (RA 8485, as amended by RA 10631), it is illegal to:

- Torture any animal
- Neglect to give an animal enough care, food or shelter, or otherwise maltreat it
- Use dogs or horses in dogfights or horsefights
- Kill an animal other than livestock like cattle, pigs, goats, poultry and rabbits, except in cases the law allows
- Use animals in research not approved by the Committee on Animal Welfare

Abandoning a pet without arranging its care is also treated as maltreatment (Section 7, added by RA 10631).

entries.q: Pets and Other Animals — Overview
entries.a: Providing regular, life-long veterinary care is important for keeping pets healthy. Contact a veterinarian if you have any questions about your pet's health or if you think your pet may be sick.

entries.q: Pets and Other Animals — How to keep pets healthy
entries.a: - Take your pet to the veterinarian for regular visits. Talk to your pet's veterinarian about how to keep your pet healthy. - Provide your pet with a good diet, fresh water, clean bedding, and plenty of exercise. - Keep up with your pet's vaccines, deworming, and flea and tick control. Fleas and ticks can spread diseases to pets and people.

entries.q: Facts About Diseases that Can Spread Between Animals and People — What to know
entries.a: - Animals, including pets, can sometimes carry germs (like viruses, bacteria, parasites, and fungi) that can make people sick. - These germs can cause many different types of illnesses in people and animals. - Animals can appear healthy even when they are carrying germs that can make people sick, depending on the disease.

entries.q: Facts About Diseases that Can Spread Between Animals and People — The basics
entries.a: There are many diseases that can spread between animals and people. These diseases are caused by harmful germs like viruses, bacterial, parasites, and fungi. These germs can cause many different types of illnesses in people and animals, ranging from mild to serious illness and even death. Animals can sometimes appear healthy even when they are carrying germs that can make people sick. People can get diseases from animals by touching an infected animal, its poop or pee, or contaminated items in its environment. See below for a list of diseases commonly associated with animals, including zoonotic, vector-borne, environmental, and other related health risks.

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — What to know
entries.a: - Pets come with many health benefits. - Pets and other animals can sometimes carry germs that can make people sick. - Young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems are more likely to get sick from these germs. - Practice healthy habits to stay healthy while enjoying pets and other animals.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Overview
entries.a: There are many health benefits of owning a pet. They can increase opportunities to exercise, get outside, and socialize. Regular walking or playing with pets can decrease blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and triglyceride levels. Pets can help manage loneliness and depression by providing companionship. Studies have shown that the bond between people and their pets is linked to several health benefits, including: - Decreased blood pressure, cholesterol and triglyceride (fat) levels, feelings of loneliness, anxiety, and symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. - Increased opportunities for exercise and outdoor activities, better cognitive function in older adults, and more opportunities to socialize. However, pets can sometimes carry harmful germs that can make us sick even when the pet appears healthy. The diseases people get from animals are called zoonotic diseases. Below are some tips to help you and your family stay healthy while enjoying pets.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Pick the right pet
entries.a: Before adopting a new pet, make sure it is the right one for you and your family. Do some research beforehand about the specific needs of the animal. Think about the animal's - lifespan - size - food, housing, and exercise needs - veterinary care costs Also consider your household members and who will be caring for the pet.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Know who is at higher risk for diseases animals can carry
entries.a: Some groups of people are more likely to get diseases spread between animals and people. These groups include children younger than 5, people with weakened immune systems, and people 65 years and older. Pregnant women are also at a higher risk for certain animal-related diseases from cats and rodents.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Wash your hands
entries.a: Washing your hands is one of the best ways to stay healthy around animals. Always wash hands after: - Touching or playing with your pet. - Feeding your pet or handling pet food. - Handling pet habitats or equipment (cages, tanks, toys, food and water dishes). - Cleaning up after pets. - Leaving areas where animals live (coops, barns, stalls), even if you didn't touch an animal. - Removing soiled clothes or shoes. Running water and soap are best for hand washing. However, you can use hand sanitizer until running water and soap are available.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Keep your pet healthy
entries.a: Regular veterinary visits are essential to keeping your pet and family healthy. Keep up with your pet’s vaccines, deworming, and flea and tick control. Talk to a veterinarian about how to keep your pet healthy. By keeping your pet healthy, you help to keep yourself and your family healthy.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Clean and disinfect
entries.a: Pets can contaminate surfaces in your home with germs. You don't have touch pets to get sick from their germs. Keep pets and their supplies out of the kitchen. Disinfect pet habitats and supplies outside the house when possible. Never clean supplies in the kitchen sink, food preparation areas, or the bathroom sink.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Pick up after your pet
entries.a: Dog and cat poop can contain parasites and germs that can be harmful to people. Always remove your dog's feces (poop) from your yard and public places. Use a bag and dispose of it in proper areas. Keep children away from areas that might contain dog or cat poop to prevent them from getting roundworms and hookworms. Cover sand boxes so cats don't use them as a litter box.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Litter boxes
entries.a: Clean the cat's litter box daily to lower the chances of exposure to harmful parasites. Pregnant women should avoid changing a cat's litter box if possible.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Teach children how to interact with animals
entries.a: Pets can teach children compassion and responsibility. However, children younger than 5 years old should be supervised while interacting with animals. This ensures the safety of the child and the pet. Teach children to wash their hands right after playing with animals or anything in the animals' environment. This includes cages, beds, and food or water dishes. Don't let children kiss pets or put their hands or other objects in their mouths after handling animals.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals — Farm animals
entries.a: Adults should supervise and be extra cautious when children younger than 5 years old have direct contact with farm animals. This includes animals at petting zoos and fairs.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Ways to Stay Healthy Around Animals

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Key points
entries.a: - Pet owners should understand how to protect their pet before, during, and after an emergency. - After an emergency, familiar scents and landmarks may change causing pets to become confused and lost. - Make a plan and create an emergency kit for your pet in case of an emergency.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Overview
entries.a: Emergencies come in many forms: fires, hurricanes, earthquakes, tornadoes, floods, violent storms, and even terrorism. Leaving pets out of evacuation plans can put pets, pet owners, and first responders in danger. Pets left behind during a disaster are likely to be injured or lost. This can happen even if you try to create a safe place for them. Be prepared: make a plan and prepare a disaster kit for your pet.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Steps to take before an emergency
entries.a: To get started, familiarize yourself with the types of disasters that could affect your area. Consider your options for providing care for your pet(s). Disasters can happen without warning, so be prepared. Make sure your pet(s) wear collars and tags with up-to-date contact information and other identification. Microchip your pet(s). This is one of the best ways to ensure you and your pet are reunited if you are separated. Always be sure to register the microchip with the manufacturer. Keep your contact information up to date with the microchip company. Keep a leash and/or carrier near the exit. Make sure you have proper equipment for pets to ride in the car (carriers, harnesses, and pet seatbelts). Prepare a Pet Disaster Kit so evacuation will go smoothly for your entire family. Ask your veterinarian for help in putting together your pet's veterinary records.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Make a plan
entries.a: Plan where you and your pet will stay in case you need to evacuate your home. Pets may not be allowed in local shelters, unless they are service animals. Many disaster evacuation centers (such as Red Cross evacuation centers) do not accept pets and other animals. Identify shelters or out-of-town friends or relatives where your pets and other animals can stay. Locate boarding facilities or animal hospitals near your evacuation shelter in the case you are unable to return home right away. Create a buddy system in case you're not home during an emergency. Ask a trusted neighbor who can check on your animals and can evacuate your animals if necessary. Find a veterinarian or animal hospital in the area where you may be seeking temporary shelter. Add the veterinarian's contact information to your emergency kit.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Create an emergency kit for your pet
entries.a: Prepare an emergency kit for your pet ahead of time with supplies, records, and contact information. Remember to write your pet's name, your name, and your contact information on each pet carrier. Include your cell, work, and home phone numbers. Include record of vaccination for rabies and other diseases, prescription medications, and medical history in your pet's medical records.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Practice evacuating your pet
entries.a: Train your pet to get in and stay in their carrier by making it a comfortable place. Practice transporting your pet by taking them for rides in a car similar to one you would be evacuating in. Make arrangements with neighbors, family, and friends if you do not have a car. You can also contact your local government to learn about transportation options during a disaster. Know where your pet might hide when stressed or scared. Practice catching your pet, if needed. For cats, you can practice removing your cat from its hiding spot. Use your cat's carrier, a pillowcase, a sturdy box, or anything to get your cat quickly out of harm's way. Have your entire family practice evacuating with your pets. This way everyone knows what to take, where to find the pets, and where to meet.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Sheltering during an evacuation
entries.a: During a disaster, what is good for you is good for your pet. If you leave your pets behind, they may be lost, injured, or worse. Never leave a pet chained outdoors. Contact your local emergency management office and ask if they offer accommodations for owners and their pets. Visit the Humane Society to find a shelter in your area. If accommodations are needed for your pet(s), contact: - Local veterinary clinics and boarding facilities - Local animal shelters - Family or friends outside the evacuation area - Pet-friendly hotels, particularly along evacuation routes Remember to take your pet's emergency kit with you.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Sheltering in place
entries.a: When sheltering at home with your pet, make sure the room chosen is pet friendly. Select a safe room, preferably an interior room with no (or few) windows. Remove any toxic chemicals or plants. Close off small areas where frightened cats could get stuck in (such as vents or beneath heavy furniture).
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Diseases that can spread between pets and people during a natural disaster
entries.a: Natural disasters can contribute to the spread of some diseases. Your pet can be put at risk for getting sick if exposed to: - Bad weather conditions - Stagnant water - Wildlife or unfamiliar animals - Overcrowding in shelters Some of these illnesses can be spread between pets and people (also known as zoonotic diseases). Common disaster-related diseases that pets can pass to people include: - Rabies - Leptospirosis - Diseases spread by mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Rabies
entries.a: Rabies is a virus that affects the nervous system in both animals and people. Rabies is transmitted through bites from rabid animals or through contact with their saliva. To protect you and your pet: - Report any bite wounds to medical personnel immediately. - Practice safe handling of pets in a stressful situation. - Keep your pet in a carrier or on a leash. - Do not allow your pet to interact with other animals.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Leptospirosis
entries.a: Leptospirosis is a bacterial disease found in the urine of infected animals. It can cause kidney damage and affect other organs. Leptospirosis is transmitted through contact with infected urine or contaminated water, soil, and food. To protect you and your pet: - Wash your hands after coming in contact with urine. - Avoid stagnant water, especially after natural disasters flooding. - Don't allow pets to play in or drink contaminated water.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Diseases spread by mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks
entries.a: Mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks are common pests of stray animals and can be a problem immediately after a disaster. Their bites irritate the skin and can also spread a variety of diseases harmful to both people and animals. These include Lyme disease and West Nile virus. To help prevent illnesses associated with mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks: - Keep your pet away from wildlife and stray animals. - Provide your pet with regular preventative care. Talk to your pet's veterinarian about regular treatment for fleas, ticks, and parasites prevention.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — How to keep yourself and your pets healthy during a disaster
entries.a: Wash your hands after handling your pet, its food, or its waste (poop and pee). Do not let your pet lick your face or hands. Keep your pet up to date on all vaccinations and heartworm, flea, and tick medicine. Practice safe handling of your pet because your pet may behave differently during a stressful situation. Keep your pet in a carrier or on a leash. Do not allow your pet to interact with other animals, especially wildlife and stray animals. Report any bite wounds to medical personnel immediately. Properly clean and disinfect cages and litterboxes. Wash your pet's bedding regularly. Avoid stagnant water, especially after flooding occurring after natural disasters. Don't allow pets to play in or drink contaminated water.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Local animal shelters
entries.a: Search for local shelters and rescue groups on Petfinder's Shelter Center. Local animal shelters may be able to offer advice during emergency situations. This includes what to do with your pets if you are asked to evacuate your home.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Relief organizations
entries.a: RedRover can shelter and care for animals displaced by natural disasters and other crises in the United States and Canada. If you need sheltering assistance, please call RedRover at (800) 440-3277 or visit RedRover.org.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — After an emergency
entries.a: After an emergency, familiar scents and landmarks may have changed. Pets can become confused and lost. It's important to keep pets on leash or in a carrier when they're being transported or when you go outside. After an emergency, especially flooding, snakes and other wildlife and downed power lines can be hazards for pets and people.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Returning home
entries.a: Check your home for sharp objects, spilled chemicals, and exposed wiring to protect your family and your pets from injury. The behavior of animals may change dramatically after a flood, flash flood, thunderstorm, or hurricane. Normally quiet and friendly animals may become irritable. Monitor animals closely and only release them in a safe and secure environment. Contact a veterinarian if you notice any signs of stress, discomfort, or illness in your pets.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Finding a lost pet
entries.a: Make sure that your family is in a safe location before you begin your search. If you are in a shelter that houses pets, inform one of the pet caretakers. Give the pet caretaker a missing pet flyer. You can also post missing pet flyers in the area once conditions are safe. Many shelters and organizations will house pets lost during disasters. The following groups can find local shelters or organizations that may have located your lost pet: - Local humane society - Animal welfare organization - County or state animal response team - Local animal control If your pet has a microchip, call the microchip company to let them know your pet is missing. Make sure all the information about your pet is updated and current.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Pet first aid
entries.a: Emergency treatment and first aid for pets should never be used as a substitute for veterinary care. However, it may save your pet's life before you can get your pet to a veterinarian. The American Veterinary Medical Association offers specific advice for basic first aid in the case of the following: - Poisoning - Seizures - Fractures - External and internal bleeding - Burns - Choking - Heatstroke They can also offer advice on what to do if your pet has no heartbeat or is not breathing.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Tips for handling injured pets
entries.a: Even the gentlest pet can bite or scratch if injured. Pain and fear can make animals unpredictable or even dangerous. Don't attempt to hug an injured pet, and always keep your face away from its mouth. Hugging an injured pet might scare the animal more or cause them pain. Perform any contact with your pet slowly and gently. Stop if your animal becomes more agitated or stressed. Try to get your pet to a veterinarian as quickly as possible without risking injury or illness to yourself or others.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA)
entries.a: AMVA offers a variety of information to assist veterinarians, animal owners, and others interested in the well-being of animals. These resources can help prepare for animal safety in the event of a disaster.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — RedRover
entries.a: RedRover Responders is a volunteer-driven organization. RedRover shelters and cares for animals displaced by natural disasters and other crises in the United States and Canada. If you need sheltering assistance, call RedRover at (800) 440-3277.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies — Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA)
entries.a: FEMA is the federal agency that leads the effort to prepare the nation for all hazards. FEMA effectively manages federal response and recovery efforts following any national incident. FEMA has resources for preparing pets for disasters.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Be Prepared: Pet Safety in Emergencies

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — What to know
entries.a: - Plan ahead of time if including pets in your travel plans. - Microchip your pet and make sure your contact information is updated. - Make sure your pet's vaccinations are up to date. - Check regulations and required documentation for your destination before traveling.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — Preparing for travel with pets
entries.a: Owning a pet can increase opportunities to exercise, get outside, and explore new places. You may want to take your pet with you when you travel to new places. Traveling can sometimes be stressful, both for you and your pets. Preparation can help prevent stress and keep you and your pets safe and healthy. Before traveling, properly identify your pet in case you get separated during your trip. Make sure your pet is microchipped for identification and keep your contact and pet information updated.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — Keeping pets safe in the car
entries.a: Having a smooth and safe road trip with your pet requires preparation and planning, especially if driving long distances. - To prepare your pet, take them on a series of short drives and gradually increase the amount of time spent in the car. - Before traveling across state lines, check the requirements for bringing pets along. - If your pet is riding on the seat, keep them in the back seat in a harness attached to the seat buckle to prevent injury. Allowing pets to roam around the car or ride with their head outside the window can be dangerous. - If your pet is kept in their crate, check that your pet can stand, sit, lie down, and turn around while inside the crate. Also, make sure the crate is well ventilated. Secure the crate so it won't slide or shift when the car stops.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — Keeping pets safe in the car
entries.a: - Bring plenty of water, food, a bowl, leash, waste bags, grooming supplies, medication and first-aid, and any travel documents including proof of rabies vaccination. Feed your pet 3 to 4 hours before leaving on your trip to prevent car sickness or vomiting. - Make frequent stops to allow dogs to go to the bathroom and stretch their legs. - Never leave your pet alone in a parked vehicle. On hot days, temperatures can rise quickly within minutes and can cause death. In cold weather, animals left in cars can freeze to death.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — International travel with pets
entries.a: Traveling with pets by plane takes careful preparation and planning and could also be costly. If you must bring your pet on a flight, here are suggestions to keep your pet safe:
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — Weeks before your trip
entries.a: - Book a direct flight when possible to decrease the chances of your pet being separated from you during extreme weather or layovers. - Check your pet's vaccinations to make sure they are up to date. Get a health certificate from your veterinarian dated within 10 days of your departure. For international travel, additional planning and healthcare requirements may be needed. Research the requirements for pets for your destination country as well as for the United States. When returning to the United States from abroad, your dog must meet all US entry requirements upon return. - For animals stowed in the plane's cargo area, purchase a US Department of Agriculture-approved shipping crate. The crate must be large enough for your pet to stand, sit, and turn around in comfortably.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — Before heading to the airport
entries.a: - Line the cargo crate with some type of bedding—shredded paper or towels—to absorb potential accidents. Place a small dish of water in the crate. Check the crate door is securely closed but not locked, so airline staff can open it in case of an emergency. - Your pet's crate should have proper identification if shipped as cargo. Mark "live animal" on the crate, and include your name, cell phone, and destination phone number.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — On the plane
entries.a: If hand-carried, never place your pet in an overhead bin. Pets must be secured in their crates below the seat in front of you in accordance with airline policies.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — Prevent injury and illness when traveling
entries.a: Practice safe and healthy habits to prevent your pet from getting sick or hurt on trips. While traveling, pets may be at greater risk for some diseases like rabies, leptospirosis, campylobacteriosis, and diseases spread by flies, mosquitoes, fleas, and ticks like New World screwworm, West Nile virus and Lyme disease. Some of these diseases can spread between people and animals. - Always supervise pets while traveling and on adventures. - Keep your pet in a carrier or on a leash. - Don't allow pets to interact with other animals, especially street dogs, stray animals or wild animals. - Don't let pets swim in, play in, or drink stagnant water or water that looks discolored, smells bad, has foam, scum, algal mats, or paint-like streaks on the surface, or has dead fish or other animals washed up on its shore or beach. Some bodies of water contain harmful algal blooms that can make people and pets sick. - Check pets for ticks after outdoor outings and talk to your veterinarian about use of a regular preventive treatment for fleas, ticks, and parasites.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: Pet Travel Safety — First aid when traveling
entries.a: Keep basic first-aid supplies for your pet in your car. You can use a travel-sized first-aid kit for your pet on flights. - Keep the phone numbers of your veterinarian, the National Animal Poison Control Center of the ASPCA (1-888-426-4435), and a 24-hour emergency veterinary hospital in the area where you will be visiting, easily accessible. - Perform a daily health check on your pet when away from home to assess their physical and behavioral changes. If you have concerns about your pet, contact your veterinarian or a local veterinarian. - Always remember: follow up any first aid administered to your pet with immediate veterinary care. First-aid care is not a substitute for veterinary care, but it may save your pet's life until veterinary treatment is available.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, Pet Travel Safety

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — What to know
entries.a: - Anyone can get sick from germs animals can carry, but some people are more likely to get sick and have more serious illness. - Riskier animals include rodents, reptiles, amphibians, and poultry. - These people don't need to avoid all contact with animals but should be aware of the risks and take steps to protect themselves.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — High-risk animals
entries.a: These animals are more likely to carry germs that can make people sick: - Reptiles and amphibians (lizards, snakes, turtles, frogs) - Backyard poultry (chickens, ducks, turkeys, geese) - Rodents (hamsters, guinea pigs, rats, mice, and other small rodents) - Exotic pets (monkeys and other wild animals) Even animals that look clean and healthy can carry harmful germs, and areas where animals live or roam can be contaminated – you don’t have to touch an animal to get sick.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — Children Younger Than 5 Years Old
entries.a: Children under 5 are more likely to get sick from germs that animals can carry. This is because young children often touch surfaces that may be contaminated with animal feces (poop), and they are more likely to put their hands in their mouths. Young children are more likely to get a serious illness from germs that animals can carry because their immune systems are still developing.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — Adults 65 and Older
entries.a: Older adults are more likely to get sick from germs some animals—even household pets—can carry, and their illness may be more severe than other people. As people age, their immune systems and organs don’t recognize and get rid of harmful germs as well as they once did.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — People with Weakened Immune Systems
entries.a: People with a weakened immune system have a higher risk of getting diseases from animals. A weakened immune system can be caused by a genetic condition, an illness such as HIV/AIDS, cancer, or kidney disease, or a treatment such as an organ transplant or radiation therapy. Some medicines can also weaken the immune system, including steroids, cancer chemotherapy, and drugs used to treat autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis or psoriasis.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — Pregnant Women
entries.a: Pregnant women are more likely than other people to get sick from certain germs animals can carry. Pregnant women can pass germs and harmful bacteria to their unborn babies or to their babies during birth. Germs, bacteria and infections can cause serious illness, birth defects, and lifelong disabilities, such as hearing loss or learning problems. Pregnant women are at risk for toxoplasmosis, which can spread from cats, and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), which can spread from some rodents.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — Petting zoos
entries.a: Every year, many people get sick after visiting an animal exhibit. From 2010-2015, about 100 outbreaks of illness in people linked to animals in public settings like zoos, fairs, and educational farms were reported to public health officials. Some of the most common harmful germs people get from animals at exhibits are E. coli, Cryptosporodium, and Salmonella.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — Schools and daycares
entries.a: There have been disease outbreaks from hatching eggs and chicks in the classroom and from contaminated animal products used for hands-on learning, such as owl pellets for dissection. Salmonella and E. coli are common germs spread by animals in these settings.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — Prevention
entries.a: Adults 65 and older, people with weakened immune systems, and caretakers for children under 5 should be aware of the increased risk of getting sick from high-risk animals. These groups might consider other animals as pets or having someone else in the household care for the animal. Everyone should wash hands thoroughly with running water and soap after handling animals, their poop and pee, their food, or other supplies. This is especially important for people at higher risk of illness.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals — How to keep kids safe
entries.a: - CDC recommends that children under 5 years old avoid contact with reptiles, amphibians, poultry (including chicks and ducklings), and rodents. - Always supervise children around animals. - Never allow children to kiss animals or to put their hands or other objects into their mouths after handling animals. - Always wash children's hands thoroughly with soap and water right after they touch, feed, or care for animals. Adults should supervise handwashing for young children. - Wash your hands before breastfeeding or preparing formula. - Keep children away from animals while they are eating to prevent the risk of bites or other injuries. - Adults should supervise and be extra cautious when children younger than 5 years old have direct contact with farm animals, including animals at petting zoos and fairs.
entries.src: CDC Healthy Pets, People at Increased Risk for Illness from Animals

entries.q: Cats — What to know
entries.a: - Cats can sometimes carry harmful germs that can make people sick. - Wash your hands after handling, cleaning up after, or feeding cats. - Provide your cat with routine veterinary care to keep it healthy and prevent the spread of diseases.

entries.q: Cats — Overview
entries.a: Nearly 40 million households in the United States have pet cats. Research has shown that cats can provide emotional support, improve moods, and contribute to the overall morale of their owners. Cats are also credited with promoting socialization among older people and physically or mentally disabled people. Although cats are great companions, cat owners should be aware that sometimes cats can carry harmful germs that can make people sick. This can happen even when they appear healthy and clean.

entries.q: Cats — Diseases
entries.a: Below is a list of diseases that can impact cats and spread to people. - Campylobacter infection - Cat scratch disease - Cat tapeworm - Cryptosporidiosis - Giardia infection - Hookworm - MRSA - New World Screwworm - Plague - Rabies - Ringworm - Roundworms - Salmonella infection - Sporotrichosis - Tickborne diseases - Toxoplasmosis - Tularemia

entries.q: Cats — Wash your hands
entries.a: Wash your hands with soap and running water: - After handling cats, their food and water dishes, or their supplies - After contact with cat saliva or poop - After cleaning a litter box - After gardening, especially if outdoor cats live in the area - Before you eat or drink Adults should supervise hand washing for children under 5 years old. Use hand sanitizer if soap and water are not readily available. Wear gloves while gardening, particularly if you know that outdoor cats live in the area.

entries.q: Cats — Safely clean up after your cat
entries.a: Cats can carry many germs in their poop. To stay healthy, take precautions when cleaning a cat's litter box. Change litter boxes daily. Always wash your hands after cleaning the litter box, even if you use a scoop to remove the poop.

entries.q: Cats — People at high risk for complications
entries.a: People with weakened immune systems and pregnant women should not clean litter boxes, if possible. They are more at risk for complications from germs spread by cats. If no one else can perform the task, wear disposable gloves and wash your hands afterwards. Keep your cat's litter box away from other animals, children, and food preparation areas.

entries.q: Cats — Prevent cat scratches and bites
entries.a: Cat bites and scratches can spread germs, even if the wound does not seem deep or serious. For example, cat scratch disease can happen if a scratch only breaks the surface of the skin. We don’t know exactly how many people are bitten or scratched by cats each year because incidents often aren’t reported. However, we do know that about 20-80% of reported cat bites and scratches become infected.

entries.q: Cats — Avoid rough play
entries.a: Avoid rough play with cats and kittens. Rough play causes cats to be defensive toward people. Avoid rough play when animals are young. This will lead to fewer scratches and bites as animals become older.

entries.q: Cats — What to do if you are bitten or scratched by a cat
entries.a: If you are bitten or scratched by a cat, you should: Wash wounds with warm soapy water immediately. Seek medical attention if: - You don't know if the cat has been vaccinated against rabies. - The cat appears sick. - The wound is serious. - The wound becomes red, painful, warm or swollen. - It has been more than 5 years since your last tetanus shot. Report the bite to animal control or your local health department if the bite is unprovoked and - The cat is a stray, or - You are unsure if the cat has been vaccinated against rabies. Cat bites carry the risk of spreading rabies to humans. Ensure the cat is seen by a veterinarian if it becomes sick or dies shortly after the bite. Report the bite by contacting your local health department.

entries.q: Cats — Before choosing a cat
entries.a: Certain types of cat or kitten adoptions may not be suitable for your family because of the risk for disease. This includes international pet adoptions. Use caution if young children, pregnant women, or people with weakened immune systems live in the household. Research and learn how to properly care for your cat or kitten before you purchase or adopt. Ask your veterinarian or pet store staff how to properly care for the cat or kitten you are selecting. This includes asking about the best food and enclosure or environment for your potential pet. Be aware that cats may shed Toxoplasma, Giardia, hookworms, roundworms and other germs in their poop. Plan to change the litterbox daily and always wash your hands after.

entries.q: Cats — How to choose a cat
entries.a: Match a cat's personality and activity levels with: - Your family, - The animals you already have in your household, and - The amount of time you have to spend with your pet. Pick a cat that is bright, alert, and playful. Cats and kittens should have shiny, soft fur that is free of poop and debris. Take your new cat or kitten to the veterinarian within a few days to a week after adoption.

entries.q: Cats — If you adopt a sick cat
entries.a: Signs of sickness in a cat include: - Appearing sluggish or depressed - Having diarrhea - Abnormal breathing - Fluid running from its eyes or nose If your cat becomes sick or dies soon after purchase or adoption, take it to the veterinarian promptly. Inform the pet store, breeder, or rescue organization about the pet's illness or death. Make sure to tell your veterinarian if the pet was adopted from a shelter or from international pet adoption.

entries.q: Cats — How to house your cat
entries.a: Provide a safe, warm, and comfortable environment for your cat to live in. Talk to your veterinarian about creating a safe environment for your cat. If you allow your cat outside, provide shelter when it is cold or rainy and shade when it is hot. Your cat should have access to the indoors at night to stay safe from predators. Make sure your cat has access to food and fresh water every day. Be aware that leaving food outdoors for your cat may attract unwanted wildlife. This wildlife can spread diseases to your cat. Each cat in a household should have its own litterbox plus one additional box.

entries.q: Cats — Monitor your cat’s health
entries.a: Take your cat to the veterinarian regularly to keep it healthy and prevent infectious diseases. Talk to your veterinarian about preventive treatments for fleas, heartworms, ticks, and other parasites. Contact your veterinarian if you notice any signs of illness in your pet. Keep in mind that even cats that look healthy can spread germs to people and other animals. Make sure to clean up any urine, poop, or vomit in the house immediately, and disinfect the area after cleaning. Make sure to wash your hands thoroughly afterwards.

entries.q: Cats — Get your cat vaccinated
entries.a: Vaccinations can help protect your cat from dangerous diseases and help them live a longer, healthier life. Keep your cat up-to-date on routine vaccinations like rabies and feline distemper vaccine. Ask your veterinarian about other vaccines you may need or want for your cat, like feline leukemia.

entries.q: Cats — Keep your veterinarian informed
entries.a: Tell your veterinarian about your cat's lifestyle. This includes whether your cat is indoor, outdoor, or both. Tell your veterinarian if there are other animals at home or that the cat may come into contact with.

entries.q: Cats — Protect your cat from ticks
entries.a: Talk to your veterinarian about the best tick prevention products for your cat and tickborne diseases in your area. Cats are extremely sensitive to a variety of chemicals. Do not apply any tick prevention products to your cat without first asking your veterinarian.
